the left and right cameras with annotated 3D bounding boxes. Each labeled key
frame is also accompanied with three adjacent unlabeled frames for providing

unlabeled video frames from 45,200 frames in the “Eigen” set.

record.title: DriveDreamer: Towards Real-world-driven World Models for Autonomous Driving

datasets.name: nuScenes
datasets.anchor:
Dataset. The training data is sourced from nuScenes [3], comprising a total of
700 training videos and 150 validation videos. Each video includes ∼20 seconds of
footage captured by six surround-view cameras. The videos have a frame rate of
12Hz, resulting in ∼1M video frames available for training. During the first-stage
training, we utilize the nuScenes-devkit [9] to acquire HDMap annotations (lane
boundary, lane divider, and pedestrian crossing) corresponding to 12Hz frames,
which are then projected onto the image plane. Considering the nuScenes dataset
only provides 2Hz 3D bounding box annotations, we supplement this with 12Hz
bounding box annotations from [70]. In the second-stage training, we employ the
yaw angle and velocity of the ego-car as the driving action inputs. Besides, we
extract scene description information (e.g., weather and time) from the nuScenes
annotation, which serves as text conditions.

datasets.name: BDD100K
datasets.anchor:
Dreamer is first pretrained on BDD100K [78] utilizing the proposed two-stage
training pipeline. Then 10K traffic conditions (from BDD100K training set) are
extracted to generate driving images. The generated images are augmented with
real images for training, and the baselines are trained for 30 epochs using the
official code [4] (see supplement for more details). The results in Tab. 2 verify
that DriveDreamer can also enhance the training of lane detection methods.

actors pass, (see Fig. 4). Each branch is simulated for N = 3 timestamps.

fall short in terms of consistency. AliO, as a loss function used in conjunction with regression loss,
aims to achieve two goals: maintaining the high accruacy of existing LTSF models while improving
their prediction consistency. Furthermore, to quantify consistency, we propose the Time Alignment
Metric (TAM). Regression metrics such as MSE, MAE, and DTW [34] represent accuracy, which is
the distance between predictions and ground truth. Therefore, they have limitations in measuring
consistency, which is a measure of performance between predictions. Complementing this, TAM
measures the distance between predictions, serving as an indicator that represents consistency.

For Perception and Reasoning, we use accuracy as the evaluation metric, as all tasks follow a

metrics.name: Robustness
metrics.anchor:
For Robustness, we evaluate a model’s ability to maintain consistent accurate predictions under color
variations. As detailed in Section 2.2, each seed image Is is transformed into n recolored variants us-
ing recoloring strategies, while keeping the original question q unchanged. A model M is considered
robust on a seed image Is and corresponding question q if and only if it provides a correct prediction
for Is and maintains correct on all n recolored versions. To quantify robustness, we define the instance-
level robustness metric R(Is, q) ∈{0, 1} and a model-level robustness metric RobustM ∈[0, 1].
